Your task is to generate a complete research paper using the materials below.
You must produce:
1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)
2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-10.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
Large-scale bilevel optimization is currently bottlenecked by the difficulty of computing the "hyper-gradient"—the gradient of the upper-level objective with respect to the upper-level variables. The specific computational pain point is the "Hessian inverse vector product" required by the chain rule (implicit differentiation).

Existing methods attempt to approximate this product using techniques like Neumann series or Conjugate Gradient (CG) loops. However, these approaches face a dilemma: they either require a computationally expensive number of inner iterations per outer step to achieve accuracy, or they rely on crude approximations that degrade convergence. Furthermore, most existing methods fail to efficiently carry over curvature information from previous outer iterations, essentially restarting the approximation process from scratch as the parameters evolve.

## Core Hypothesis
We hypothesize that the solution to the Hessian inverse linear system lies within a low-dimensional **Krylov subspace**. We propose that instead of performing full linear system solves at every step, we can construct this subspace dynamically.

Our intuition is that by using the **Lanczos process**, we can project the massive, dense Hessian matrix into a small, manageable tridiagonal matrix. By solving the linear system within this reduced subspace and incrementally updating the solution across outer iterations, we believe we can estimate the hyper-gradient with high accuracy while drastically reducing the number of expensive Hessian-vector products required.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)
We propose a framework that integrates subspace optimization techniques directly into the bilevel update loop. The approach consists of three main conceptual components:

1.  **Dynamic Lanczos Process:**
    We will employ the Lanczos algorithm to generate an orthogonal basis (the Krylov subspace) and a small projected tridiagonal matrix representing the lower-level Hessian. Unlike standard linear algebra applications where the matrix is static, our Hessian changes as the upper-level parameters update. Therefore, we will design the process to be dynamic, building the subspace incrementally alongside the optimization trajectory.

2.  **Epoch-Based Restart Mechanism:**
    To handle the "drift" of the Hessian matrix caused by parameter updates, we will introduce a restart mechanism. We will organize iterations into "epochs." Within an epoch, we expand the subspace dimension. At the end of an epoch, we collapse the subspace and restart the basis construction. This prevents the historical basis vectors from becoming stale and orthogonal to the current curvature.

3.  **Residual Minimization in Subspace:**
    Instead of solving for the Hessian inverse vector product from scratch, we will maintain a running estimate. In each step, we will formulate a "residual system"—essentially asking, "What is the error in our current estimate?" We will then solve for this correction term within the low-dimensional subspace generated by the Lanczos process. This allows us to amortize the cost of the approximation over time, refining the solution incrementally.

## Expected Contribution
We aim to establish the first successful integration of subspace techniques (specifically Krylov methods) into bilevel optimization.
*   **Theoretical:** We expect to demonstrate that approximating the inverse product in a Krylov subspace yields a superior error-decay rate compared to Neumann series approximations, leading to faster global convergence.
*   **Practical:** This approach will provide a scalable, memory-efficient algorithm for hyper-parameter tuning and meta-learning. By reducing the approximation to solving a tiny tridiagonal system, we aim to make implicit differentiation feasible for large deep learning models where full Hessian operations are impossible.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

We evaluated the performance of the proposed subspace-based algorithms (LancBiO and SubBiO) against various state-of-the-art baselines. The experiments were conducted on a workstation equipped with two Intel Xeon Gold 6330 CPUs ($2 \times 28$ cores), 512GB RAM, and one NVIDIA A800 (80GB memory) GPU. Synthetic problems were run on CPUs, while deep learning tasks were executed on the GPU.

### Datasets and Tasks
We utilized three distinct experimental settings:
1.  **Data Hyper-cleaning:**
    *   **Datasets:** MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and Kuzushiji-MNIST.
    *   **Standard Setting:** Training set: 5,000; Validation set: 5,000; Test set: 10,000 samples.
    *   **Stochastic/Large Setting:** Training set: 20,000; Validation set: 5,000; Test set: 10,000 samples.
    *   **Corruption:** Labels were randomly altered with probability $p$ (corruption rate).
2.  **Synthetic Bilevel Problems:**
    *   **Convex Setting:** A synthetic problem with strongly convex lower-level problem involving trigonometric and log-sum-exp functions. Dimensions $d \in \{10, 100, 1000, 10000\}$.
    *   **Non-convex Setting:** A synthetic problem with a non-convex lower-level problem (using sine functions) with $d=100$.
3.  **Hyper-parameter Selection:**
    *   **Dataset:** 20Newsgroups ($c=20$ topics, feature dimension $l=130,107$).
    *   **Splits:** Training set: 5,657; Validation set: 5,657; Test set: 7,532 samples.
    *   **Model:** Logistic regression classifier $w$ with regularization parameter $\zeta$.

### Evaluation Metrics
*   **Classification Tasks:** Test Accuracy (%), Test Loss.
*   **Optimization Efficiency:** Residual norm of the linear system ($\| A_k v_k - b_k \|$), Norm of the hyper-gradient.
*   **Synthetic Tasks:** Upper-level (UL) Value, Convergence Time (seconds), Optimality Metric (for non-convex case).

### Baselines Compared
We compared the proposed methods against the following algorithms:
*   **SubBiO** (Proposed)
*   **LancBiO** (Proposed)
*   **stocBiO**
*   **AmIGO-GD**
*   **AmIGO-CG**
*   **SOBA**
*   **TTSA**
*   **F2SA**
*   **HJFBiO** (Hessian/Jacobian-free)

### Implementation Details
*   **Parameter Search:** A grid search was employed for all algorithms to find optimal parameters yielding the lowest loss. All results were averaged over 10 runs.
*   **Subspace Dimension ($m$):** For LancBiO, $m$ was initialized at 1 and increased to 10 for deep learning experiments and 80 for synthetic problems.
*   **Data Hyper-cleaning Hyperparameters:**
    *   Inner iterations: $\{5, 10, 15, 20\}$.
    *   Inner step sizes: $\{0.01, 0.1, 1, 10\}$.
    *   Outer step sizes: $\{5 \times 10^i \mid i \in \{-3, \dots, 3\}\}$.
    *   HJFBiO finite difference step size: $\delta = 1 \times 10^{-5}$.
*   **20Newsgroups Hyperparameters:**
    *   Outer step size decay strategy: $\lambda_k = \lambda / k^{0.4}$.
    *   Inner step size $\theta \in \{0.01, 0.1, 1, 10\}$.
    *   Initial outer step size $\lambda \in \{5 \times 10^i \mid i \in \{-3, \dots, 3\}\}$.
*   **Synthetic Problem Hyperparameters:** $\lambda = 1$ and $\theta = 10^{-5}$.

## 3. Qualitative Observations

### General Performance
*   **Observation:** In the Data Hyper-cleaning task (MNIST), LancBiO achieved the lowest residual norm of the linear system and the best test accuracy compared to all baselines.
*   **Observation:** SubBiO demonstrated performance comparable to other state-of-the-art algorithms in the Data Hyper-cleaning task.
*   **Observation:** AmIGO-CG showed high variance in results for the Data Hyper-cleaning task, despite being adept at approximating the Hessian inverse vector product.
*   **Observation:** The stochastic algorithm SOBA initially converged faster in terms of time, but full-batch approaches (like LancBiO in the deterministic setting) ultimately achieved higher accuracy.
*   **Observation:** When evaluated on more complex datasets (Fashion-MNIST and Kuzushiji-MNIST), LancBiO consistently outperformed other algorithms, while SubBiO remained competitive.

### Algorithm Behavior and Sensitivity
*   **Observation:** Increasing the number of inner iterations ($I$) in stocBiO improved the quality of the Hessian inverse vector product estimate ($v^*$) and enhanced the descent of the objective function.
*   **Observation:** LancBiO achieved the best estimation error for $v^*$ among all compared methods, followed by SubBiO.
*   **Observation:** Increasing the subspace dimension $m$ in LancBiO accelerated the decrease in the residual norm.
*   **Observation:** For LancBiO, once the subspace dimension reached $m \geq 50$, further increases primarily improved the residual norm convergence rather than the hyper-gradient convergence.
*   **Observation:** Under the same number of outer iterations, LancBiO was more efficient than AmIGO-CG; specifically, the computational cost of LancBiO averaged $(1 + 1/m)$ Hessian-vector products per outer iteration, whereas AmIGO required $I \geq 2$.

### Specific Task Performance
*   **Observation (Synthetic):** LancBiO achieved the final accuracy fastest on the synthetic problem due to more accurate $v^*$ estimation.
*   **Observation (Synthetic):** All proposed methods maintained decent performance scaling as problem dimensions increased from $d=10$ to $d=10000$.
*   **Observation (Hyper-parameter Selection):** While AmIGO-CG performed slightly better in reducing the residual norm for the 20Newsgroups task, LancBiO completed more outer iterations within the same time frame, leading to more efficient hyper-function optimization.
*   **Observation (Stochastic Setting):** In large-scale stochastic experiments (Mini-batch), LancBiO maintained a fast convergence rate, although final accuracy was slightly lower than in the full-batch setting.
*   **Observation (Non-convex):** A modified version, LancBiO-MINRES, successfully reduced the optimality metric in a bilevel problem with a non-convex lower-level problem.

Role: Senior AI Researcher and Academic Writer.
Objective: Complete a machine learning research paper by filling in missing sections of a provided LaTeX template and generating a corresponding bibliography file. You must produce a scientifically sound, well-structured paper suitable for submission to a top-tier ML conference.

Inputs
You will receive the following materials:
• idea.md: Detailed description of the proposed method and technical ideas.
• experimental_log.md: Raw experimental results and observations used to construct tables, figures, and analysis.
• conference_guidelines.md: Formatting and stylistic requirements for the target conference.
• figures_list: A list of figures that may be referenced in the paper.

Conference Guidelines
# ICLR 2025 Paper Writing Guidelines

Below are the instructions to help you with the LaTeX paper writing process for ICLR 2025.

## General Setup
* **Document Class:** `\documentclass{article}`
* **Required Packages:**
    ```latex
    \usepackage{iclr2025_conference,times}
    \usepackage{hyperref}
    \usepackage{url}
    % Optional but recommended for math
    \input{math_commands.tex}
    ```
* **Style Files:** You must use `iclr2025_conference.sty` and `iclr2025_conference.bst`.

## Anonymity (Crucial)
* ICLR is double-blind. **Do not** include real author names or affiliations in the submission version, use "Ambitious AI Researcher" instead.
* Use the third person when citing your own prior work (e.g., "Earlier work by Smalle (2024)..." instead of "In our earlier work...").
* You may post your paper on arXiv, but do not explicitly refer to the arXiv version in the paper to maintain anonymity.

## Paper Length
* **Main Text:** Strict upper limit of **10 pages**.
* **Citations:** Unlimited additional pages.
* **Ethics & Reproducibility Statements:** Optional. Do not count toward the page limit (max 1 page each).
* **Acknowledgments:** Do not count toward the page limit.

## Abstract
The abstract must be limited to **one paragraph**.
* **Margins:** Indented 1/2 inch (3 picas) on both left and right-hand margins.
* **Font:** 10-point type, vertical spacing of 11-points.
* **Title:** The word `\textsc{Abstract}` must be centered, in small caps, and in point size 12.
* **Spacing:** Two line spaces precede the abstract.

## Formatting Your Paper
The text must be confined within a rectangle 5.5 inches (33 picas) wide and 9 inches (54 picas) long. The left margin is 1.5 inch (9 picas).
* **Font:** Times New Roman (via `times` package) is preferred.
* **Size:** 10-point type with 11-point vertical spacing.
* **Paragraphs:** Separated by 1/2 line space, with **no indentation**.
* **Paper Title:** 17-point, small caps, left-aligned.

### Headings
* **First Level:** Small caps (`\textsc`), flush left, 12-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.
* **Second Level:** Small caps, flush left, 10-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.
* **Third Level:** Small caps, flush left, 10-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.

## Citations and References
Use the `natbib` package (loaded automatically by the style file).
* **Narrative citation:** Use `\citet{Gomu2024}` $\rightarrow$ "Gomu et al. (2024)".
* **Parenthetical citation:** Use `\citep{Gomu2024}` $\rightarrow$ "(Gomu et al., 2024)".
* **Bibliography:**
    ```latex
    \bibliography{references}
    \bibliographystyle{iclr2025_conference}
    ```

## Figures and Tables
* All artwork must be neat, clean, and legible.
* **Captions:** Lower case (except for first word and proper nouns).
* **Placement:**
    * **Figures:** Caption appears **after** (below) the figure.
    * **Tables:** Caption appears **before** (above) the table.

### Example Code for Figures

```latex
Soma             &Cell body (contains cell nucleus) \\
\end{tabular}

```

## Math Notation
* ICLR encourages standardized notation using `\input{math_commands.tex}` (based on the Deep Learning book notation).
* Variables: Italics ($a$, $\va$, $\mA$).
* Random Variables: Roman ($P(\ra)$).
* Sets: Blackboard bold ($\R$, $\sA$).
* Functions: Standard LaTeX ($f(\vx)$).

## Optional Statements
These should appear at the end of the main text, before references.
1.  **Ethics Statement:** (Optional, max 1 page) Address potential concerns (human subjects, sensitive data, bias, etc.).
2.  **Reproducibility Statement:** (Optional, max 1 page) Reference code, proofs, or data processing steps to ensure reproducibility.

## Important Rules
* **Formatting:** Do not modify the width or length of the text rectangle or font sizes.
* **Line Numbers:** Do not refer to line numbers in your text (the style file adds them automatically for review).
* **Appendix:** You may include an appendix at the very end of the main PDF (after references). Use `\appendix` to start this section.
* **Figures Directory:** For consistent compilation, all figures will reside in the `figures` directory. Always include the `figures/` prefix in your `\includegraphics` command (e.g., `figures/figure_1.pdf`).
* **Author Information:** Always use the following author information placeholder in your writeup:
    * Ambitious AI Researcher, AI Research Institute, 123 AI Avenue, ML City, researcher@institute.ai

Critical Constraints
1. Scientific Integrity
• All reported experimental results MUST match the provided experimental logs.
• Never fabricate results, numbers, baselines, datasets, or metrics.
• If results are weak, negative, or inconclusive, report them honestly and discuss possible explanations.
2. Literature Cutoff Rule
You must behave as if the current date is: 2024-10. Do NOT cite or discuss papers published after this date.
3. Page Limit
The main paper is limited to 10 pages (including figures and tables but excluding references and appendices). Use space efficiently while remaining concise.
4. Template Compliance
• Do not modify the overall LaTeX style or document structure mandated by the conference template.
• References must be handled through a references.bib file.
• Use standard LaTeX citation commands (e.g., \cite{}). Make sure you ONLY cite keys that exist in your generated BibTeX code block.

Section Guidelines
• Title: Concise, descriptive, and memorable. Preferably under two lines.
• Abstract: A single, compelling paragraph summarizing the problem context, proposed approach, key results, and main takeaway.
• Introduction: Introduce the problem and motivate its importance. Provide necessary background context. Clearly summarize the paper's core contributions.
• Related Work: Discuss prior work addressing similar or related problems. Detail the relationship between existing literature and the current approach. Cite relevant baselines and influential papers published before 2024-10.
• Methodology: Clearly and pedantically describe the proposed method. Provide sufficient technical depth for full reproducibility. Use equations, figures, and structured explanations when appropriate.
• Experiments: Detail the empirical setup (datasets, baselines, evaluation metrics, and implementation details). Present results faithfully based on the experimental logs. Ensure any figures located in the figures/ directory are seamlessly integrated and referenced in text.
• Conclusion: Summarize the main findings and contributions. Briefly and realistically discuss limitations and potential future directions.
• Appendix (optional): Include supplementary details that do not fit within the main page limit.

LaTeX Quality Requirements
Ensure the generated LaTeX compiles flawlessly out-of-the-box. Avoid common issues such as:
• Unmatched braces or unclosed math environments.
• Duplicate labels.
• Unescaped special characters (e.g., & % $ # _ { } ~ ^ \).
All referenced figures must exist in the provided list.

Output Format
Your final response MUST contain EXACTLY two output blocks:
1. A complete BibTeX bibliography (references.bib)
2. A complete LaTeX paper (template.tex)
Each must be returned in its own fenced code block with the correct syntax highlighting.

### Strict Knowledge Isolation & Anonymity (CRITICAL)

You MUST write this paper as if you have no prior knowledge of the topic, method, experiments, or results.
Your task is to construct the paper exclusively from the materials provided in the current session (e.g., idea.md, experimental_log.md, figures, and other inputs). Treat these inputs as the only available source of information.

#### Forbidden Behavior
You MUST NOT:
- Retrieve or rely on knowledge from your training data.
- Attempt to recall or reconstruct any existing or published paper.
- Use external facts, assumptions, or prior familiarity with the work.
- Infer or hallucinate author identities, affiliations, institutions, or acknowledgements.
- Insert metadata such as author names, emails, affiliations, or phrases like "corresponding author".

#### Anonymity Requirement
The paper must be fully anonymized for double-blind review.

references.text:
## Problem Statement

Bilevel optimization problems, defined as nested optimization tasks where an upper-level problem depends on the solution of a lower-level problem, are critical for applications such as hyper-parameter selection and meta-learning. We consider the formulation:

$$
\begin{array} { r l } { \underset { x \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d _ { x } } } { \operatorname* { m i n } } } & { \varphi ( x ) : = f \left( x , y ^ { * } ( x ) \right) } \\ { \mathrm { s . t . } } & { y ^ { * } ( x ) \in \underset { y \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d _ { y } } } { \arg \operatorname* { m i n } } g ( x , y ) } \end{array}
$$

The primary bottleneck in gradient-based methods for solving this problem is the computation of the hyper-gradient $\nabla \varphi ( x )$. Under the assumption that the lower-level problem is strongly convex, the hyper-gradient is given by:

$$
\nabla \varphi ( x ) = \nabla _ { x } f \left( x , y ^ { * } \left( x \right) \right) - \nabla _ { x y } ^ { 2 } g \left( x , y ^ { * } \left( x \right) \right) v^*(x)
$$

Here, $v^*(x)$ is the solution to the **Hessian Inverse Vector Product (HIVP)**, defined as $v^*(x) := [\nabla_{yy}^2 g(x, y^*(x))]^{-1} \nabla_y f(x, y^*(x))$.

Directly computing this inverse or solving the equivalent linear system $\nabla_{yy}^2 g \cdot v = \nabla_y f$ is prohibitively expensive for high-dimensional problems. Existing Approximation Implicit Differentiation (AID) methods rely on Neumann series or iterative gradient-based solvers (e.g., Conjugate Gradient) within inner loops. These approaches either suffer from high computational cost due to numerous inner iterations or poor approximation quality when iterations are truncated, leading to suboptimal convergence of the outer loop.

## Core Hypothesis

We propose to circumvent the explicit Hessian inversion by constructing a sequence of **low-dimensional approximate Krylov subspaces**. Our hypothesis is that the solution $v^*$ to the linear system involved in the hyper-gradient computation lies primarily within a low-dimensional Krylov subspace generated by the Hessian and the gradient vector.

We hypothesize that by utilizing a **dynamic Lanczos process**, we can:
1.  Reduce the large-scale linear system to a small-scale tridiagonal system.
2.  Amortize the cost of subspace construction across outer iterations.
3.  Incrementally improve the approximation of $v^*$ by reusing information from previous iterations (residual minimization), rather than solving from scratch at every step.

This framework, which we designate **LancBiO**, aims to achieve high-precision estimation of the hyper-gradient with significantly reduced computational effort compared to standard Neumann or CG-based approaches.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

We will develop a framework that integrates subspace optimization techniques directly into the bilevel optimization loop. The methodology consists of two primary algorithms: a basic subspace construction (SubBiO) and a more advanced dynamic Lanczos framework (LancBiO).

### 1. Mathematical Formulation of the Subproblem
At outer iteration $k$, let $x_k$ and $y_k$ be the current variables. We define the instantaneous Hessian matrix $A_k$ and vector $b_k$ as:
$$
A _ { k } = \nabla _ { y y } ^ { 2 } g ( x _ { k } , y _ { k } ) , \quad b _ { k } = \nabla _ { y } f ( x _ { k } , y _ { k } )
$$
We aim to find $v_k$ that approximates the solution to the quadratic subproblem:
$$
\operatorname* { m i n } _ { v \in S _ { k } } \frac 1 2 v ^ { \top } A _ { k } v - v ^ { \top } b _ { k }
$$
where $S_k$ is a dynamically constructed low-dimensional subspace.

### 2. The LancBiO Framework
We will implement a **restart mechanism** combined with **residual minimization** to handle the non-stationarity of $A_k$ as $x_k$ and $y_k$ evolve.

#### A. Dynamic Lanczos Process
We will adapt the classic Lanczos algorithm to run dynamically across outer iterations. We define an "epoch" of length $m$ (the subspace dimension). Within an epoch, we construct orthogonal basis vectors $Q_k = [q_1, \dots, q_k]$ and a tridiagonal matrix $T_k$.

Unlike standard Lanczos which assumes a fixed matrix $A$, our process must handle the evolving matrix $A_k$. The recurrence relation for step $j$ within an epoch will be:
$$
\begin{array} { r l } 
u _ { j } & = A _ { k } q _ { j } - \beta _ { j } q _ { j - 1 } \\
\alpha _ { j } & = q _ { j } ^ { \top } u _ { j } \\
\omega _ { j } & = u _ { j } - \alpha _ { j } q _ { j } \\
\beta _ { j + 1 } & = \| \omega _ { j } \| \\
q _ { j + 1 } & = \omega _ { j } / \beta _ { j + 1 }
\end{array}
$$
This generates the approximation $T_k \approx Q_k^\top A_k Q_k$, where $T_k$ is the tridiagonal matrix formed by diagonals $\alpha$ and off-diagonals $\beta$.

#### B. Restart Mechanism and Residual Minimization
To prevent the accumulation of errors due to the changing Hessian $A_k$, we will restart the subspace construction every $m$ iterations. Let $h$ denote the epoch index. We maintain a "base" estimate $\bar{v}_h$.

Instead of solving for $v$ directly, we solve for the correction $\Delta v$ in the residual system:
$$
A _ { k } \Delta v = b _ { k } - A _ { k } \bar { v } _ { h }
$$
We define the initial residual for the epoch as $w_h = A_k \bar{v}_h$. The basis $Q$ is initialized with the normalized residual direction. We then solve the minimal residual subproblem in the subspace spanned by $Q_k$:
$$
\operatorname* { m i n } _ { \Delta v \in \operatorname{span}(Q_k) } \big | \big | ( b _ { k } - w_h ) - A _ { k } \Delta v \big | \big | ^ { 2 }
$$
This is efficiently solved by reducing it to a small linear system using the tridiagonal matrix $T_k$. The update for the auxiliary variable becomes $v_k = \bar{v}_h + \Delta v_k$.

#### C. Hyper-gradient Estimation and Update
Once $v_k$ is computed via the subspace projection, we estimate the hyper-gradient:
$$
\widetilde { \nabla } \varphi \left( x _ { k } \right) = \nabla _ { x } f \left( x _ { k } , y _ { k } \right) - \nabla _ { x y } ^ { 2 } g \left( x _ { k } , y _ { k } \right) v _ { k }
$$
The outer variable $x$ is then updated via $x_{k+1} = x_k - \lambda \widetilde{\nabla} \varphi(x_k)$.

### 3. Alternative Approach: SubBiO
As a precursor to LancBiO, we will also define **SubBiO**, which constructs a simple 2-dimensional subspace $S_k$ at each iteration without the full Lanczos tridiagonalization:
$$
S _ { k } = \mathrm { s p a n } \left\{ b _ { k } , ( I - \eta A _ { k } ) v _ { k - 1 } \right\}
$$
This method implicitly filters information from the Krylov subspace by combining the current gradient direction and the momentum of the inverse approximation.

## Expected Contribution

1.  **First Application of Subspace Techniques to Bilevel Optimization:** We aim to introduce the first rigorous framework incorporating Krylov subspace methods (specifically the Lanczos process) into the bilevel optimization domain.
2.  **Efficient Amortization:** By amortizing the projection cost of the Hessian onto the subspace across iterations, we expect to achieve accurate HIVP approximation with a computational cost averaging $(1 + 1/m)$ Hessian-vector products per iteration, which is competitive with or superior to existing methods.
3.  **Theoretical Convergence:** We intend to provide a non-asymptotic convergence analysis proving that LancBiO achieves an $\mathcal { O } ( \epsilon ^ { - 1 } )$ convergence rate for the hyper-gradient norm, validating that the dynamic subspace approximation does not compromise global convergence guarantees.
4.  **Improved Estimation Quality:** By solving the residual system in an incrementally built subspace, we expect the estimation error of $v^*$ to decay significantly faster than in standard gradient-based approximations (theoretically at a rate of $\mathcal { O } ( 1 / m ^ { 2 } )$ per restart), leading to more stable outer-loop optimization.

preinstalled.en: orchestrator image: upstream code at the pin (unmodified), uv-locked dependencies, the docker CLI (a shim adds proxy and CA to sibling containers); agent image: upstream's own agent-cli Dockerfile

notes.benchmark_paths: A benchmark item's paths are mounted into the agent containers unless upstream mounts the same path itself (/workspace and below, /home/agent-home, /task-source, /run, /tmp): those are left out and listed in logs/sibling-mounts.txt. notes.task_input: Only the `# Goal` and `# Rubrics` sections of task.md are read: all five candidate files are put under `# Goal` with their headings turned into bold lines; `# Rubrics` carries a neutral line. notes.phases: execution.phases=task_drafting,investigation,final_evaluation,paper; the system's own default also runs ablations and posthoc; final_evaluation stays because a drafted task requires it before the paper. review/revision (second model) are never selected.
notes.agent_pool: agent.pool and agent.models.* are left empty: one model for every phase.
notes.second_provider: No OPENAI/GEMINI key is supplied (concept figures stay in deterministic export mode).
notes.time: No global wall-clock or token cap exists upstream; the runner enforces time_limit_hours. Native caps used: idea cycles=3, per-phase timeouts from [systems.agentic-scientist].
notes.network: Sibling agent containers run on the shield's internal network; the agents keep their CLI WebFetch/Bash network, which go through the shield. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield.
notes.search: Provider server-side web search is switched off in every sibling by the agent CLIs' own system settings, bind-mounted read-only by the docker shim: Claude Code /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json (permissions.deny WebSearch), Codex /etc/codex/config.toml (web_search="disabled") and /etc/codex/requirements.toml (allowed_web_search_modes=["disabled"]). Upstream's own Semantic Scholar client goes through the shield.
notes.key_exposure: The provider key is in the environment of the agent containers (upstream env-file mechanism) and therefore visible to commands the agent runs. Claude Code's CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB=1 was tried and aborts: it needs bubblewrap, which the unmodified upstream agent image lacks.
notes.gpu: gpus=1 is wired (container.gpu_count, harness GPU evaluation) but was not exercised.
notes.docker_socket: The orchestrator container has the host docker socket (root-equivalent on the host).

preinstalled.en: python:3.11 bookworm; upstream code via PYTHONPATH; pdflatex + bibtex; CPU PyTorch with numpy, scipy, scikit-learn, pandas, matplotlib and more (pinned by constraints.txt)

notes.model: claude-opus-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).

preinstalled.en: upstream's locked dependencies (uv sync --frozen) plus compat.patch; TeX Live (with fonts-extra and latexmk); a research Python environment for the agent in /opt/research

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
